# Schema commands: entities, read, fields, field-create, field-update, field-delete

## `fptctl schema entities`

List every entity type and its properties.

Prints what the library's schema_entity_read returns: each entity type's display name, visibility and other properties. With --project, the schema as that project sees it.

```text
fptctl schema entities [OPTIONS]
```

Library call: `Shotgun.schema_entity_read`.

Options:

- `--project Project:ID|JSON`: Read or change the schema as seen by a project.

Examples:

```shell
fptctl schema entities
fptctl schema entities --project Project:70
```

## `fptctl schema field-create`

Create a field on TYPE and print its name.

TYPE is an entity type, DATA_TYPE a field data type such as text, number, list or entity, and DISPLAY_NAME the name people see. The server derives the field name (sg_...) from DISPLAY_NAME. --properties sets more, such as {"valid_types": ["Asset"]} for an entity field.

```text
fptctl schema field-create [OPTIONS] TYPE DATA_TYPE DISPLAY_NAME
```

Library call: `Shotgun.schema_field_create`.

Options:

- `--properties JSON|@FILE|-`: More field properties.
- `--dry-run`: Print the library call instead of making it.

Examples:

```shell
fptctl schema field-create Shot text "Review notes"
fptctl schema field-create Shot entity "Hero asset" --properties '{"valid_types": ["Asset"]}'
```

## `fptctl schema field-delete`

Delete FIELD from TYPE.

TYPE is an entity type and FIELD the field name. The field goes to the site's Trash, and its name stays taken until someone deletes it there for good in the web UI. On a terminal, field-delete asks for confirmation; anywhere else it needs --yes.

```text
fptctl schema field-delete [OPTIONS] TYPE FIELD
```

Library call: `Shotgun.schema_field_delete`.

Options:

- `--yes`: Do not ask for confirmation.
- `--dry-run`: Print the library call instead of making it.

Examples:

```shell
fptctl schema field-delete Shot sg_review_notes --yes
```

## `fptctl schema field-update`

Change the properties of FIELD on TYPE.

TYPE is an entity type and FIELD the field name. --properties gives the properties to set as a JSON object, such as {"description": "..."}. With --project the change applies to that project only, for the properties that can differ per project, such as visible.

```text
fptctl schema field-update [OPTIONS] TYPE FIELD
```

Library call: `Shotgun.schema_field_update`.

Options:

- `--properties JSON|@FILE|-`: Properties to set. [required]
- `--project Project:ID|JSON`: Read or change the schema as seen by a project.
- `--dry-run`: Print the library call instead of making it.

Examples:

```shell
fptctl schema field-update Shot sg_review_notes --properties '{"description": "From review"}'
fptctl schema field-update Shot sg_review_notes --project Project:70 --properties @hide.json
```

## `fptctl schema fields`

Read the fields of TYPE, or only FIELD.

TYPE is an entity type and FIELD a field name such as sg_status_list. Each field comes with its data type, whether it is editable, its valid values and its other properties. With --project, the fields as that project sees them.

```text
fptctl schema fields [OPTIONS] TYPE [FIELD]
```

Library call: `Shotgun.schema_field_read`.

Options:

- `--project Project:ID|JSON`: Read or change the schema as seen by a project.

Examples:

```shell
fptctl schema fields Shot
fptctl schema fields Shot sg_status_list --project Project:70
```

## `fptctl schema read`

Read the whole schema: every field of every entity type.

The result is large, so prefer `schema fields` for one entity type. With --project, the schema as that project sees it.

```text
fptctl schema read [OPTIONS]
```

Library call: `Shotgun.schema_read`.

Options:

- `--project Project:ID|JSON`: Read or change the schema as seen by a project.

Examples:

```shell
fptctl schema read --project Project:70
```
